hooks.text: A truck-sized fireball skipped off our atmosphere in 1972.
How did a massive space rock bounce off Earth and escape?
One hundred seconds in the air before skipping back to space.

title: The Fireball That Skipped Off Earth
description: Discover the 1972 Great Daylight Fireball, a massive space rock that bounced off Earth's atmosphere like a skipping stone.

beats.text: A truck-sized fireball skipped off our atmosphere in 1972.
beats.visual: Artist concept of an Earth-grazing meteoroid in the upper atmosphere, 1972

beats.text: Most space rocks this size either incinerate or blast a massive crater into the ground.
beats.visual: Artist concept of a meteoroid exploding in the air vs impacting the ground, 2020

beats.text: But on August 10, this rock entered the atmosphere directly over Utah.
beats.visual: Map showing the trajectory of the 1972 fireball over North America, 1972
queries: Map of western United States and Canada

beats.text: Moving at 15 kilometers per second, it glowed bright enough for tourists to film.
beats.visual: Photograph of the Grand Teton mountain range landscape behind Jackson Lake, 1972

beats.text: Military satellites tracked the object for 100 seconds as it skipped like a stone.
beats.visual: Infrared view of North America from an orbital weather satellite, 1972
queries: Weather satellite view of North America

beats.text: Instead of crashing, the meteoroid merely grazed the atmosphere and rebounded into space.
beats.visual: Illustration of a meteoroid skipping off the atmosphere and escaping into space, 1972

beats.text: Astronomer Zdenek Ceplecha later determined this brief encounter permanently shifted its solar orbit.
beats.visual: Orbital diagram of an Apollo-type near-Earth asteroid crossing Earth's orbit, 1994

beats.text: Not a single solid fragment reached the ground after skipping off the atmosphere and escaping into space.
beats.visual: Close-up studio photograph of a stony meteorite specimen showing its crust, 1994
